title: Percolation of a rod-like particle in a static bed of spheres: trapping and passing
authors: Juan C. Petit, Julio M. Ottino, Richard M. Lueptow, Paul B. Umbanhowar
abstract: We numerically investigate percolation of independent frictionless glued-sphere rod-like particles under gravity through a disordered static bed of larger spheres. We identify two distinct regimes: a \emph{trapping} regime, where rods stop after percolating a limited distance in the bed and a \emph{passing} regime, where rods percolate continuously with constant mean velocity. The transition between these regimes is governed by the length of the rod and the geometrical trapping threshold for spherical particles based on the rod diameter and the minimum pore throat diameter defined by three touching large spheres. The percolation velocity for all rod geometries, including the single sphere limit, collapses onto a single curve when scaled with the gravitational acceleration and the bed sphere diameter. The results also demonstrate that short rods percolate nearly twice as fast as long rods due to the geometric constraints associated with the disordered pore structure of the static bed. Consequently, long rods are more susceptible to trapping via specific contact configurations with the bed spheres, which differ from those for short rods. These results reveal how shape anisotropy introduces dynamical constraints and thresholds in granular percolation, with implications for predicting segregation in mixtures of non-spherical particles.
summary: This work numerically investigates how rod-shaped particles move through a fixed bed of spheres, revealing two key behaviors: getting permanently stuck (trapping) or moving continuously (passing). The results show that particle shape anisotropy introduces strong dynamical constraints, causing longer rods to slow down and become more easily trapped than shorter ones.
main_problem: The study investigates the percolation behavior of rod-like particles moving through a static, disordered bed of larger spheres under gravity.
main_result: Two distinct regimes—trapping and continuous passing—are identified, with percolation velocity depending strongly on particle aspect ratio and pore geometry. Longer rods are found to be more susceptible to geometric trapping than short rods.
method: The research relies heavily on Discrete Element Method (DEM) simulations to model the mechanical interactions between the rod-like particles and the static sphere bed.
model_or_system: The system consists of frictionless, non-interacting rod-like particles percolating through a disordered packing ($\phi=0.60$) of larger spheres. The rods are modeled as collinear small spheres, and dynamics are governed by linear spring-dashpot contact forces.
key_observables: Trapping probability ($N_{	ext{trap}}/N$), characteristic penetration length ($\lambda$), percolation velocity ($	ilde{v}_p$), mean contact number ($\langle Z angle$), and rod orientation distributions $P(	heta)$.
important_parameters: Rod aspect ratio ($A$ or $L^*$), size ratio ($R = d_L/d_S$), gravitational acceleration ($g$), and the geometrical trapping threshold ($R_t$).
main_assumptions: Frictionless contacts are assumed for the primary analysis, and rod-rod interactions are disabled in some simulations. The system is treated as quasi-static or governed by constant mean velocity in the passing regime.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the initial packed bed structure ($g(r)$), the exponential decay of trapping probability vs. depth, phase diagrams mapping trapping/passing regimes based on particle geometry, and orientation distributions for trapped versus percolating rods.
paper_structure: The paper systematically analyzes the transition between trapping and passing states by varying rod length and size ratio, quantifying this transition using scaling laws derived from simulation data, and analyzing local contact geometries to explain the observed dynamical constraints.
why_interesting: While focused on granular physics, the study models complex non-equilibrium transport phenomena in disordered media. The identification of distinct dynamic regimes (trapping vs. passing) governed by geometric thresholds has parallels in understanding energy dissipation or flow through porous quantum structures.
